processing: Mature, later-picked leaf and stem is withered and dried like other white teas, and much of it is then steamed and pressed into cakes.
harvest_season: Late, after bai mu dan and gong mei, using more mature leaf. Autumn pressed lots are also sold, often labelled by solar term such as Bai Lu.
appearance_dry: Large, mixed leaves and stems in olive, brown and gold, whether loose or pressed.
appearance_liquor: Deeper gold to amber, with more body than higher white grades.
appearance_wet: Big, broad leaves and pieces of stem in olive-brown.
taste_profile: Sweet hay, dried fruit and honey in a fuller body, gaining date notes with some years of storage.

brewing.notes: Hot water and short early steeps suit it. It also takes well to simmering once it has a few years on it.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, loose or often pressed into cakes. It is the grade most often bought for keeping: a few years in, it gains date and honey character, while young lots are cheaper and brighter. Check the claimed year, as older ones get faked.
description:
Shou mei is the big-leaf, big-stem end of white tea, and the Fuding version is what many people now buy as an everyday or storage tea. It lacks the prestige of silver needle, but it often has more to say in the cup.

The process is the same wither and dry, only with older leaf, more stem and later picking. That extra maturity gives a darker cup and more body. Pressing makes it easy to store, and it is said to slow change in a dry climate.

Fresh, expect sweet hay and honey; with some years, date and dried fruit. Use hot water and do not fear stems, which add sweetness. A pot simmered from an older cake is one of the great cold-weather uses for it.

Definitions overlap: sources disagree on how shou mei and gong mei differ, though gong mei is usually thought of as finer. Very low grades look heavy with black-red leaves and may taste flat, so choose even leaf that smells clean.
history: Shou mei is one of the standard grades of Fujian white tea, set by the maturity of the leaf, and Fuding-area production is usually placed after the earlier spring pickings. A separate dated history of the Fuding version is little documented. Pressed shou mei cake is described by some as traditional, but pressing it for storage has clearly become a common way to sell the grade.
